# R7 Digest — Return & Sheba (2 Sam 19–20)
Source: Tsumura, *The Second Book of Samuel* (NICOT)
Cache slice: `R7_return_sheba_19-20_9682-11168.txt`
Raw lines covered: **9682–11168** (slice-internal L1–~738 body; endnotes L740+ are prior-ch. apparatus, not extracted as claims)
Declared scope: David’s grief aftermath; return to Jerusalem; Judah/Israel dispute; Sheba revolt; Joab kills Amasa; officers list (19–20).

---

### C-R7-01
**Claim:** David’s private grief for Absalom turns the day’s military victory into public mourning; the people “steal” into the city as if humiliated in defeat rather than celebrating.
**Quote:** “And the victory that day became mourning for all the people, for the people heard that day, ‘The king is in pain concerning his son.’ And the people stole into the city that day, as people do who are humiliated when they flee in battle.”
**Locus:** 19:1–3 [MT 2–4]; slice L2–12; Tsumura on 18:33–19:8
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-02
**Claim:** Tsumura frames the grief scene as the conflict between David as king and David as father—a theme running through Absalom’s rebellion from ch. 13 (and 1 K. 1:6); David lets grief overcome kingly responsibilities and gratitude for salvation.
**Quote:** “David lets his own grief overcome his kingly responsibilities, and even his gratitude to God for his salvation. The conflict between David as king and David as father is a theme throughout the story of Absalom’s rebellion, actually from chapter 13, as well as 1 K. 1:6.”
**Locus:** Tsumura comment on 18:33–19:8; slice L72–73
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-03
**Claim:** David’s lament is elevated poetry (four-line parallelism; “my son” ×5, “Absalom” ×3; chiastic structure) that formally emphasizes his anguish; he goes to the gate chamber for privacy, not to perform ANE roof funeral rites (de Ward / Keret parallel noted and rejected).
**Quote:** “David’s lament is highly elevated poetry, a four-line parallelism with the repetition of my son (5×) and Absalom (3×) and a chiastic structure. … There is no mention of David’s performing any rite; he is simply convulsed with emotion. He probably went to the gate chamber because it was the nearest place he could be private.”
**Locus:** Tsumura on 18:33 / 19:4; slice L74–77, L19–20
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-04
**Claim:** Joab rebukes David as pragmatic, basically true though exaggerated: by covering his face in grief David has “covered with shame” the faces of servants who saved him and his household; David loves those who hate him and hates those who love him—if Absalom lived and they all died, David would be pleased.
**Quote:** “Today you have covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who today have saved your life… by loving those who hate you and by hating those who love you. … that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased.”
**Locus:** 19:5–6; slice L22–47; Tsumura L81–83
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[joab]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-05
**Claim:** Tsumura reads Joab’s rebuke as accusing David of violating the king–subject covenant of reciprocal loyalty-love (not vassal-suzerain per Olyan, nor primarily patron-client per Hobbs); 1 Sam. 10:25 and 2 Sam. 5:3 imply such a covenant.
**Quote:** “Joab’s words also accuse David of violating the covenant between a king and his subjects — the love of loyalty should be repaid with the love of loyalty. … the relationship here is not that between kings or between patron and client, but the ‘king-subject’ relationship. 1 Sam. 10:25 and 2 Sam. 5:3 seem to imply a covenant.”
**Locus:** Tsumura on 19:5; slice L83–84
**Targets:** [[joab]], [[david]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-06
**Claim:** Joab swears that if David does not go out and “speak to the hearts” of his servants, no man will stay that night—worse than all evil from David’s youth; David then arises, sits in the gate, and the people come before him.
**Quote:** “And now, arise, go out, and speak to the hearts of your servants, for I swear by the LORD, if you do not go out, not a man will stay with you this night. … And the king arose and sat in the gate. … And all the people came before the king.”
**Locus:** 19:7–8; slice L49–69; Tsumura L87–89
**Targets:** [[joab]], [[david]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-07
**Claim:** At Joab’s words David puts emotions under control, behaves as king sitting in the gate (royal/judicial seat; Iron Age gate canopy base at Dan noted); next he must reunite the country.
**Quote:** “At these words, David puts his emotions under control. He makes his peace with his men, behaving as king, sitting in the gate. … Now David has to work on reuniting the country.”
**Locus:** Tsumura on 19:8; slice L87–89
**Targets:** [[david]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-08
**Claim:** Section 19:9–43: the whole country agrees to bring David back, but this exposes Judah/Israel division. Israel (northern tribes) had spoken about return; David makes a special appeal to Judah; a Judean contingent accompanies him without consulting other tribes; at the Jordan he meets figures from the flight (Shimei, Ziba, Mephibosheth, Barzillai); Israel and Judah then bicker over the triumphal return.
**Quote:** “The whole country finally agrees they should bring David back, but even this creates problems as it shows up the division between Judah and the rest of Israel. … So a Judean contingent comes and accompanies David back, apparently without consultation with the other tribes.”
**Locus:** Tsumura intro to 19:9–43; slice L91–93
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Shimei; Ziba; Mephibosheth; Barzillai

### C-R7-09
**Claim:** All the tribes of Israel dispute among themselves: David delivered them from enemies and Philistines; he fled from Absalom; Absalom, “whom we anointed,” is dead—so why silence about bringing the king back?
**Quote:** “It was the king who delivered us from the hand of our enemies; it was he who saved us from the hand of the Philistines. But now he has fled out of the land from the side of Absalom. As for Absalom, whom we anointed over us, he is dead in battle. Now, why are you silent about bringing the king back?”
**Locus:** 19:9–10; slice L97–113; Tsumura L161 (anointing probably at Hebron sacrifices 15:10–12; no explicit mention in narrative)
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-10
**Claim:** David sends Zadok and Abiathar to the elders of Judah: why last to bring the king back when all Israel’s word has already come? “You are my kin; you are my bone and flesh.” Judah, where the revolt began (15:10), is slower than Israel; may have been divided pro-/anti-David while Israel was more united.
**Quote:** “Why are you the last to bring the king back to his house, while the word of all Israel has come to the king… You are my kin; you are my bone and flesh.” … “Judah, where the revolt began (15:10), was slower in reclaiming David as its king than was Israel.”
**Locus:** 19:11–12; slice L115–133; Tsumura L165–167
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-11
**Claim:** David orders the priests to tell Amasa he will be army commander “in place of Joab”—an oath “May God do so to me, and more.” Demoting the victorious loyal general for the defeated rebel general seems shocking; Tsumura suggests David may have cited Joab’s disobedience re Absalom (18:5) and necessity to unite the nation.
**Quote:** “Are you not my bone and flesh? May God do so to me, and more, if you will not be the army commander before me from now on, in place of Joab.” … “To demote the victorious loyal general in favor of the soundly defeated rebel general (17:25) seems shocking. Perhaps David pointed out to Joab that he had disobeyed his specific order about Absalom (18:5).”
**Locus:** 19:13; slice L135–144; Tsumura L169–171
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[joab]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Amasa

### C-R7-12
**Claim:** Hearts of all Judah are turned “as one man”; they invite David to return; king comes to the Jordan; Judah comes to Gilgal to meet him and bring him across. MT *wayyaṭ* is impersonal passive “hearts … were turned,” not requiring emendation to Amasa as agent (contra McCarter / NRSV “Amasa swayed”).
**Quote:** “Thus the hearts of all the men of Judah were turned as one man. And they sent (messengers) to the king, (saying) ‘Return, you and all your servants.’ … the agent of the verb ‘to turn’ has been defocused and hence 3 m.s. of the verb is used impersonally … So there is no need to emend the MT as McCarter does.”
**Locus:** 19:14–15; slice L146–155; Tsumura L173–175 (Gilgal cultic center near Jericho; location uncertain)
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-13
**Claim:** Transition 19:16–18a: Shimei son of Gera (Benjamite of Bahurim) hurries with men of Judah and a thousand Benjaminites; Ziba with fifteen sons and twenty servants rushes to the Jordan; a crossing is set up for the royal household. 18a is a HINGE connecting Ziba/Shimei’s haste with the sons-of-Zeruiah debate over Shimei’s fate.
**Quote:** “And Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite, who was from Bahurim, hurried and came down with the men of Judah to meet King David; and there were a thousand men of Benjamin with him. As for Ziba… they rushed down to the Jordan… A crossing was set up… It is probably a HINGE connecting the quick movements by Ziba and Shimei with the following discussion…”
**Locus:** 19:16–18a; slice L177–191
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Shimei; Ziba

### C-R7-14
**Claim:** Shimei falls before David at the Jordan, confesses sin on the day David left Jerusalem, and presents himself as first of “all the house of Joseph” to meet the king. Tsumura: “house of Joseph” = northern tribes vs. house of Judah (Benjamin as Joseph’s brother).
**Quote:** “May my lord not consider me guilty, nor remember what your servant did wrong on the day when my lord the king went out of Jerusalem… For your servant knows that I myself sinned; so, here I have come today, as the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king.” … “The house of Joseph here refers to all the northern tribes in contrast to ‘the house of Judah’…”
**Locus:** 19:18b–20; slice L203–223; Tsumura L251
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Shimei

### C-R7-15
**Claim:** Abishai demands Shimei’s death for cursing “the LORD’s anointed”; David rebukes the sons of Zeruiah as adversaries (*śāṭān*) and refuses executions on the day he knows he is king over Israel; he swears Shimei shall not die. Tsumura: day of rejoicing not retribution; but David “apparently did not forgive him from the heart” (1 K. 2:8–9, 36–46). McCarter links “today I am king” with coronation amnesty (cf. 1 Sam. 11:13–15).
**Quote:** “Should not Shimei be put to death for this? For he cursed the LORD’s anointed.” … “What is it to me and to you (pl.), O sons of Zeruiah, that you should become an adversary to me today? Should anyone be put to death in Israel today? For do I not know that today I am king over Israel?” … “You shall not die.” And the king swore to him. … “David wants this to be a day of rejoicing, not retribution. He apparently did not forgive him from the heart, however (see 1 K. 2:8-9, 36-46).”
**Locus:** 19:21–23; slice L225–247; Tsumura L249–257
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[joab]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Shimei; Abishai

### C-R7-16
**Claim:** Mephibosheth comes unkempt (feet, beard, clothes unwashed from king’s departure until safe return)—signs of mourning/loyalty. He claims Ziba deceived him (took the donkey; slandered him); flatters David as “like the angel of God”; recalls Saul’s house were “dead men” until seated at David’s table.
**Quote:** “He had not taken care of his feet, nor trimmed his beard; and he had not washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he came home safely. … ‘O my lord, the king, my servant deceived me… And he has slandered your servant… But my lord the king is like the angel of God… For all the house of my father were nothing but dead men to my lord the king, but you set your servant among those who ate at your table.’”
**Locus:** 19:24–28; slice L261–293; Tsumura L309–327
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-17
**Claim:** Narrator does not adjudicate Mephibosheth vs. Ziba outright, but Tsumura holds v. 24 suggests the narrator believes Mephibosheth (donkeys scarce even for royal household in 16:1–2). David’s verdict—“You and Ziba shall divide the land”—suggests uncertainty; McCarter thinks David believes Mephibosheth but is grateful for Ziba’s help. Mephibosheth offers Ziba all the land if the king is safely home.
**Quote:** “The narrator does not state directly which is telling the truth — after all, he may not have had direct information — but v. 24 suggests that he believes Mephibosheth. … ‘You and Zibah shall divide the land.’ … It is difficult to decide which David believes here. His verdict … suggests that he is not sure, but McCarter thinks he believes Mephibosheth, but is grateful for Ziba’s help.”
**Locus:** 19:24–30; Tsumura L309–331; verdict L295–307
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Mephibosheth; Ziba

### C-R7-18
**Claim:** Barzillai the Gileadite (eighty; great man who sustained David at Mahanaim) escorts David to the Jordan but declines Jerusalem hospitality—cannot enjoy food, drink, or singers; prefers to die in his city near parents’ grave. Offers Chimham (likely son/grandson; cf. 1 K. 2:7) in his place; David kisses and blesses Barzillai; Chimham goes on with him.
**Quote:** “You cross over with me, and I will sustain you in Jerusalem with me.” … “Today I am eighty years old. … Why should your servant still become a burden to my lord the king? … Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city, near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham…” … “David never forgot Barzillai’s help.”
**Locus:** 19:31–40; slice L335–399; Tsumura L401–409
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-19
**Claim:** Men of Israel accuse Judah of “stealing” the king at the Jordan; Judah answers kinship and no royal favoritism (“eaten at the king’s expense”); Israel claims “ten shares in the king” and priority for first speaking of return. Judah’s words are “more severe.” Singular pronouns mark acrimonious debate.
**Quote:** “Why have our kindred the men of Judah stolen you away…?” … “I have ten shares in the king; yea, in David I have more than you. … Did I not speak the first words about bringing back my king?” And the words of the men of Judah were more severe than the words of the men of Israel.
**Locus:** 19:41–43; slice L417–447
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-20
**Claim:** Tsumura: David left Mahanaim too quickly for northern accompaniment; northerners resent Judah “privatizing” the king. Judah sees David as their man who became king; Israel sees a God-chosen king of all Israel with equal tribal shares. David tried (Jerusalem capital; ark) not to be merely a Judahite king, “but he was not able to overcome the division.” Rivalry leads into Sheba’s revolt.
**Quote:** “Apparently, David left Mahanaim and came to the Jordan without leaving time for the northern tribes to come and accompany him. … In making Jerusalem his capital and bringing the ark there, David seems to have made effort to be not a Judahite king ruling Israel, but an Israelite king. However, he was not able to overcome the division. … this rivalry between Israel and Judah for priority in bringing David back leads up to Sheba’s revolt in the following chapter.”
**Locus:** Tsumura on 19:41–43; slice L449–463
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-21
**Claim:** Sheba’s revolt (20:1–22) connects directly to the prior split; little support beyond his clan (v. 14), but northern resentment lingered, grew under Solomon (Judah omitted from food-levy list 1 K. 4:7–19), and culminated in the split under Rehoboam (1 K. 12).
**Quote:** “Sheba’s revolt is directly connected with the split within the country in the previous paragraph. It does not seem to have gained support outside of his own clan (v. 14), but even after this, the feeling that the king was not treating them well seems to have lingered among the northern tribes, increased under Solomon … and finally ended up causing the nation to split in two (1 K. 12).”
**Locus:** Tsumura intro to 20:1–22; slice L465–467
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Sheba

### C-R7-22
**Claim:** Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite “worthless fellow” (*ʾîš belîyaʿal*), blows the trumpet and cries: “No portion is there for us in David; no share for us in the son of Jesse. Everyone to his own tent, O Israel!” All Israel withdraws after him; Judah clings to David from Jordan to Jerusalem. Cry summons old tribal independence; repeated under Rehoboam (1 K. 12:16).
**Quote:** “No portion is there for us in David; no share for us in the son of Jesse. Everyone to his own tent, O Israel!” … “Sheba seems to say, ‘If we don’t have ten shares, we have none.’ … Everyone to his own tent is a summons to resume the old tribal independence. This rallying cry is repeated over forty years later during the reign of Rehoboam (1 K. 12:16).”
**Locus:** 20:1–2; slice L471–487
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Sheba

### C-R7-23
**Claim:** David, back in Jerusalem, sequesters the ten concubines Absalom had taken (15:16; 16:22) in a guarded house with provision but no conjugal access—life-long widows (*ʾalmenût ḥayyût*, “widowhood of livingness”).
**Quote:** “And the king took the ten women, the concubines whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in a guarded house and provided for them, but he did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, as life-long widows.”
**Locus:** 20:3; slice L491–497
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-24
**Claim:** David orders Amasa to muster Judah in three days (short if all Judah); Amasa delays. David tells Abishai Sheba may do more harm than Absalom and to pursue with “your lord’s servants” (standing army). Tsumura: David overestimates Sheba; v. 2’s “all Israel followed” is largely going home; only Bichrites/Beerites actively follow (v. 14).
**Quote:** “Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. As for you, take your lord’s servants and pursue him.” … “David fears that his kingdom is dangerously fragile. However, he seems to have overestimated Sheba’s strength. … everyone except the Bichrites, the members of Shiba’s own clan, seems to have acted neutral (v. 14).”
**Locus:** 20:4–6; slice L501–519; Tsumura L561–571
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-25
**Claim:** Joab’s men (plus Cherethites, Pelethites, mighty men) go out; Joab effectively co-leads with Abishai as usual. At Gibeon’s large stone Joab greets Amasa as “my brother,” seizes his beard to kiss, and strikes him in the belly with the (left-hand) sword so that bowels pour out—one blow kills. Parallel to Joab’s murder of Abner (3:27); “brother” may mark first-cousin kinship.
**Quote:** “Is it well with you, my brother?” And Joab’s right hand took hold of Amasa’s beard to kiss him. But Amasa did not notice the sword that was in Joab’s hand. And he struck him in the belly with it. And his inward parts poured out on the ground. Though he did not strike him again, he died. … “The killing of Amasa shows how ruthless Joab could be with a rival; compare his revenge on Abner in 3:27.”
**Locus:** 20:7–10; slice L521–541; Tsumura L559, L579
**Targets:** [[joab]], [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Amasa; Sheba; Abishai

### C-R7-26
**Claim:** A Joabite stands by the corpse: “Whoever favors Joab, whoever is for David, let him follow Joab”—while Amasa wallows in blood mid-road until the body is moved to the field and covered; only then do men pass after Joab. Addressees/stoppers are likely Amasa’s Judahite levy (v. 4).
**Quote:** “Whoever favors Joab, whoever is for David, let him follow Joab,” while Amasa was wallowing in his blood in the middle of the approach road. … “The people who are addressed and who stopped are probably the ‘men of Judah’ of v. 4 who had come with Amasa from Judah to Gibeon.”
**Locus:** 20:11–13; slice L543–555; Tsumura L587
**Targets:** [[joab]], [[david]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Amasa

### C-R7-27
**Claim:** “All the men of Israel” in 20:2 is hyperbole; Sheba’s path through the tribes to Abel Beth-maacah shows no organized national revolt—only Beerites assemble and follow. Abel = Tell Abil el-Qamḥ (~7 km WNW of Dan). Tsumura prefers Beerites (Asherite/northern association) over LXX-based “Bichrites.”
**Quote:** “The phrase all the men of Israel in v. 2 is a hyperbole. The present section shows that there was no organized ‘revolt’ by Sheba; only the ‘Beerites’ followed him, as he went through all the tribes of Israel … and through all the Beerites.”
**Locus:** 20:14; Tsumura L595–599; site L595
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Sheba

### C-R7-28
**Claim:** Siege of Abel of Beth-maacah: earthwork (*sōlēlâ*) against the rampart; people with Joab attack/undermine the wall. A wise woman (comparable to Abigail 1 Sam. 25 and Tekoa’s woman 2 Sam. 14) summons Joab; Abel was proverbially a place of inquiry that settles matters.
**Quote:** “And they came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah and heaped up an earthwork against the city… And a wise woman called from the city… ‘Formerly they indeed used to say, “Let them surely inquire at Abel”; thus they finished the matter.’” … “This speech of the wise woman can be compared with those by Abigail in 1 Sam. 25:24-31 and the wise woman of Tekoa in 2 Sam. 14:4ff.”
**Locus:** 20:15–18; slice L603–639; Tsumura L673–685
**Targets:** [[joab]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-29
**Claim:** Wise woman claims to be among the “peaceable and faithful in Israel”; accuses Joab of seeking to destroy a “mother city” (*ʿîr weʾēm*, hendiadys for metropolis) and swallow “the inheritance of the LORD” (covenant people and promised land). Joab disclaims destruction; demands only Sheba, who “has lifted up his hand against King David.” City throws Sheba’s head over the wall; Joab trumpets dispersal and returns to Jerusalem to the king.
**Quote:** “You are seeking to destroy a mother city in Israel. Why will you swallow up the inheritance of the LORD?” … “But a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose name is Sheba the son of Bichri has lifted up his hand against King David. Give up only him…” … “they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it to Joab… As for Joab, he returned to Jerusalem to the king.”
**Locus:** 20:19–22; slice L640–671; Tsumura L687–693
**Targets:** [[joab]], [[david]], [[2-samuel]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R7-30
**Claim:** Tsumura: rebellion of Sheba closes the story of Absalom’s revolt (13:1–20:26). David apparently did not punish Joab for Amasa’s murder (Joab still commander at end of reign, 1 K. 1:19) but did not forgive him either (1 K. 2:5–6); 1 K. 2:5 shows David blamed Joab for what ensued.
**Quote:** “The rebellion of Sheba is the close of the story of Absalom’s revolt in 13:1-20:26.” … “Apparently, David did not punish Joab for the murder of Amasa, as he was commander at the end of David’s reign (1 K. 1:19), but he did not forgive him either (1 K. 2:5-6).” … “First Kings 2:5 shows that he blamed Joab for what ensued…”
**Locus:** Tsumura on 20:4–22 and 20:22; slice L559, L693, L571
**Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[joab]], [[david]], [[absalom]], [[david-tsumura]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]
**Misc flags:** Amasa; Sheba

### C-R7-31
**Claim:** Officers list 20:23–26 parallels 8:16–18 and Solomon’s officials 1 K. 4:1–6; posts overlap largely but order differs; this list does not open with the king. Usual surmise: ch. 8 = early reign; ch. 20 = later years (Adoram continues under Solomon; forced-labor office absent from ch. 8).
**Quote:** “This list is very similar to the list in 8:16-18 and the one of Solomon’s officials in 1 K. 4:1-6. The posts and officials overlap to a large degree, but the order is different, and the one in this chapter does not start out with the king, unlike the others. It is usually surmised that the list in 2 Sam. 8:16-18 is from the early years of David’s reign, and the list in the present passage is from the later years…”
**Locus:** 20:23–26; Tsumura L720–723

### C-R7-32
**Claim:** Roster: Joab over all the army of Israel; Benaiah over Cherethites and Pelethites; Adoram over forced labor (*mas*/corvée—state institution sometime in David’s reign, cf. 12:31; Adoram later stoned under Rehoboam, 1 K. 12:18 = Adoniram 1 K. 4:6); Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud recorder; Sheva scribe; Zadok and Abiathar priests; Ira the Jairite a priest for David (private chaplain/advisor type; cf. 8:18 / Solomon’s “priest and king’s friend”).
**Quote:** “Now Joab was over all the army of Israel; Benaiah the son of Jehoiadah was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; Sheva was scribe; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; Ira the Jairite also was a priest for David.” … “The corvée apparently became a state-organized institution in Israel sometime during David’s reign (see 12:31).”
**Locus:** 20:23–26; slice L703–717; Tsumura L725–737
